items.title: Elizabeth Holmes' fiance is the worst man in America. Now we have him on tape.
items.content:
NOTE: This review contains spoilers for “You Can See Everything.”

Sometimes the best journalists are people who don’t even purport to be journalists. The late Anthony Bourdain was one such accidental herald, as was “Borat” star Sacha Baron Cohen before the gonzo comedian became recognizably famous no matter his alter ego. Let’s go ahead and add writer/performer Nathan Fielder to the list. You and I know Fielder best from “Nathan For You” and “The Rehearsal.” Everyone else is about to know him for “You Can See Everything,” a tag team effort with documentarian Lance Oppenheim that is not only the best film of 2026 so far, but also one of the finest works of journalism I’ve ever seen.

This movie arrives in theaters with plenty of deserved Oscar buzz. But in this case, a mere filmmaking award seems insufficient in recognition. As far as I’m concerned, this thing deserves a Pulitzer (categories be damned). And maybe a Nobel Prize.

Article continues below this ad

But I’m getting ahead of myself. In case you haven’t seen the film’s trailer, “You Can See Everything” is a portrait of infamous Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted in 2022 of defrauding her company’s investors and is currently in prison in Texas. You can read all about Holmes in John Carreyrou’s book “Bad Blood,” an essential tick-tock of the Theranos scandal. The book not only tells the story of how Holmes led people to believe that her company’s revolutionary blood-testing hardware worked (it did not), but also of how the greater Silicon Valley culture inspired Holmes, and in some cases perhaps abetted her. The Theranos scandal was one of the highest profile financial scandals of this century, and Holmes was the haunting, unblinking face of it.

Holmes went dark for years after her malfeasance was exposed, until she and her fiance, Billy Evans, agreed to let Fielder and Oppenheim into their slipshod rental cottage in Del Mar for weeks on end and film the couple (and their two very cute children) as they prepared for Holmes to report to prison. Fielder and Oppenheim were allowed to film the Holmes family nearly 24/7, with Fielder at one point agreeing to stay with the family for an extended period of time. Hence, the film’s title. You will, indeed, see everything. Almost too much of everything, given that this doc runs nearly three hours, and given that the camera stays uncomfortably tight on its participants, Fielder included, for the bulk of that time.

You’ll also see Billy Evans’ penis, so be warned or titillated as you see fit.

Article continues below this ad

As Fielder ingratiates himself with Holmes and Evans, he gets them comfortable enough to ask the hard questions: about Theranos, about prison, and even about themselves. The resulting footage is often shocking. You will see Elizabeth Holmes, who still maintains she did nothing wrong, answer “no” when Fielder asks her if she’s ever lied in her life. You will hear Billy Evans, the real villain in this particular story, tell everyone in the room that he carries a gun on him 24/7. You will see Fielder screen the legendary “Who’s on first?” sketch for Holmes and her partner, with Holmes missing the central joke of the sketch entirely. You will see Fielder explain to Holmes that “Who” is the name of the guy on first base, with her still not really grasping it. And you’ll see Holmes’ partner tell her, “You see the world differently,” in a skin-crawling attempt to turn her seeming cluelessness into something laudatory. The Silicon Valley mindset at work.

Speaking of the Valley mindset, you will also see Holmes and Evans spend a great deal of time in this movie attempting to boot up Theranos 2.0. They even go so far as to drag out some of the original Theranos blood testing apparatus, which looks like a bunch of random parts from TigerDirect they hooked together, to show Fielder what their product can do. We do not see it doing anything on screen, but the couple assures that it would if it was, like, hooked up properly. 

These scenes are extremely funny, but funny isn’t what Fielder is looking for. He’s trying to figure out if this woman is a clueless naif, if she believes her own lies, or if she is playing the of an innocent woman, and doing so with such effectiveness that, to paraphrase Fielder, she might be the most manipulative person in the world.

Article continues below this ad

The answer proves fabulously elusive, and so Fielder and Oppenheim go to extremes in their attempt to find it. They hold the camera on Holmes’ rubbery elfin face for what feels like hours at a time, to see if she’ll blink (figuratively literally!). They interview Holmes’ visiting parents, with the father, former Enron exec Christian Holmes, casually telling Fielder that everything changed for his daughter “when she was raped.” To the furthest extreme, they bring in actress Amanda Seyfried — who  Holmes in the Hulu TV show “The Dropout” — to recreate any dialogues Fielder had with Holmes herself that couldn’t be recorded on camera. Seyfried is so convincing in mimicking Holmes that you, the audience, might forget which scenes were Seyfried talking to the camera and not Holmes herself. I know I did.

It gets crazier. After Holmes reports to prison, Seyfried joins Fielder on a trip to visit Billy Evans in a clandestine attempt to get Holmes’ partner to admit that, without Holmes’ knowledge, he demanded (and for a moment, received promise of), monetary compensation from the A24 studio for the couple’s participation in this documentary.

A brief pause here. Billy Evans is scion to the San Diego-based Evans Hotels family fortune. Evans met Holmes well after she’d become notorious, but tells Fielder early in “You Can See Everything” that he didn’t recognize her when the two first met. In fact, he fell in love with Holmes within an hour of meeting her, then found out who she was, still wanted to be with her anyway. Do you buy this story? Of course you don’t. This man is full of s—t, and that becomes even more apparent when he’s confronted by both Fielder and Seyfried after Holmes has reported to prison. That’s when we hear Evans sneer, “I’m better read than you,” at Seyfried — who, as a reminder, is one of the most skilled people in the world at her chosen profession. He also taunts Seyfried for getting “owned” on Twitter after she derided the late white supremacist Charlie Kirk, whom of course Evans actually admired. This man is an absolute piece of s—t.

Thankfully, Seyfried says as much, becoming audience surrogate after that alarming sequence and telling Fielder that Holmes’ partner is “bats—t crazy.” Amanda Seyfried might be the coolest person in Hollywood. As for Fielder, he’s left wondering if Holmes has been victimized by her own partner, by her former Theranos paramour Sunny Balwani (also now in prison, and whom Holmes also accused of raping her), and by God knows who else. Was this woman, once a billionaire, more pawn than mastermind? Fielder shows some (platonic) fondness for Holmes over the course of this film, but by this point in the story it’s hard to know if , the interviewer, is also playing a character in order to get what he wants.

Article continues below this ad

Fielder, to his credit, acknowledges the thorniness of all this. He’s openly uncertain of having Seyfried dramatize Holmes’ words on camera because, no matter how talented the actress is, it’s still not Holmes herself saying those words to the camera. He also doesn’t know if he’s surreptitiously fallen for Holmes’ graciousness, to the point where he questions himself to Seyfried for believing Holmes when she told him, almost on a lark, that she had no clue Evans was making money moves behind her back. That leads to Seyfried herself wondering if her own Hulu portrayal of Holmes was truth, blurred truth, or just fiction. By the end of the film, Seyfried isn’t sure what the word “fiction” should even mean.

That’s what makes this film a masterwork. “You Can See Everything” refers plainly to the extensive footage that Fielder and Oppenheim were able to obtain. But here’s a documentary that also shows you, the audience, its whole methodology. It allows you to see the potential flaws in its reporting, and how those flaws might impede the filmmakers’ attempt to find real answers. 

It’s that truly radical transparency that differentiates this documentary not only from the tacit sponcon docs that now plague your television (Billy Evans cites Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s deal with Netflix as a reason that he should be paid by A24 for appearing on camera), but also from a lot of the best pure documentaries ever filmed. Here is a movie that exists on a level with Banksy’s “Exit Through the Gift Shop” as a superlative example of how the truth can be not just impossible to find but, with great determination, can be eradicated altogether. I’ll never forget it.

items.title: Steve Hilton is convinced he's going to win. Hahahaha.
items.content:
There’s a midterm election coming on Nov. 3, which includes a race here in California to determine who will replace Gov. Gavin Newsom. On the blue side of the ticket is unremarkable Democrat Xavier Becerra, whose chief positive attribute is that he is not a Republican. On the red side is Steve Hilton, an immigrant from the U.K. who gained U.S. citizenship in 2021. Hilton’s most high-profile political experience came back in the early 2010s, when he served as an adviser to then-U.K. prime minister and alleged porcine enthusiast David Cameron. But that experience, plus a lengthy stint as a commentator for Fox News, was enough to convince Hilton that he not only should run for governor, but that he WILL be the state’s next governor.

On the surface, he makes for an attractive candidate. Hilton is good company, and when I met him, he was as good at explaining the issues, as you would expect a seasoned broadcaster to be. He’s even reaching out to the gay community, albeit in somewhat awkward fashion. Listen to the man talk and you might come away thinking he’s a Democrat.

But Steve Hilton is not a Democrat. He’s a Republican, one who plans to give tax breaks to the wealthy, massively increase funding to the police and let artificial intelligence companies do basically whatever they want without fear of California regulation. Most importantly to me, he is backed by President and aspiring dictator Donald Trump. So, Hilton can’t run as a Republican, especially not in a state as firmly blue as California, without having to answer for that party’s standard-bearer. But God bless Hilton, he gave it a try, repeatedly, when I met with him in August. This was true right from my opening question, when I asked him why he wanted to run for governor here at all.

Article continues below this ad

“I love California and it’s obviously not working,” he told me. “Sixteen years of one-party rule, it’s a disaster. So we’ve got to turn things around.”

“OK,” I shot back, “but why would I trust a Republican to change any of this, in this administration?”

At this, Hilton feigned ignorance. “In which administration?”

Article continues below this ad

“The Trump 2 administration.”

“I don’t see the relevance of that to California.”

Hilton acknowledged none of those things. Instead, he continually portrayed himself as a heroic outsider. “I’m not the president,” he insisted, with a showman’s vigor. “I’m not him. I’m me.”

Article continues below this ad

When I brought up the president later in our conversation, he complained to me, “I don’t know why you keep talking about Trump.”

“That’s why I’m here,” I told him. “Because you’re a Republican. I want you to explain to me how you could possibly exist as a functional Republican with the standard-bearer of that party exercising a ridiculous amount of influence over the party and being a general, omniscient presence over the entire country, California included.”

“Well, I think that description, it just doesn’t match the facts,” Hilton told me. The polls at the time implied that voters did not agree. When I met Hilton in August, he was trailing Becerra badly, so I asked him why he was running a campaign that was doomed to fail. 

“That gap [in the polls] is shrinking,” he said to me, with no lack of confidence. “The gap went from 25 to 18 in the Berkeley poll. What was the next one? Our own internal poll, down to 14 points. There’s a poll that we’re hearing about next week where the gap will be under 10%.” 

Article continues below this ad

Hilton didn’t mention that he was quoting polls from before and after the primary, and the gap fell from 21 not 25, which is VERY much a Republican thing for him to do, but I still gave him the benefit of the doubt.

“Let’s say the poll numbers hold and you don’t win the election,” I said to him. “Where would you go after this?”

At this, he laughed. “I don’t know. I haven’t thought about it. I’m planning to win. I do believe that I’m going to be the next governor. I can see it. I believe it.”

Article continues below this ad

“Is that your ego talking? Have you convinced yourself?”

“No, it’s California talking. It’s the conditions in our state.”

“It’s not the polls talking.”

“Yes, but we’re just at the start of the campaign. No one really pays attention until after Labor Day anyway. Everything points to this being a change election in California. That means that I will win the election. That is my strong expectation.”

Article continues below this ad

But that confidence only holds if Hilton pretends the Trump factor in this race isn’t significant. Surely the voters he’d met along the trail had told him as much. That’s why I asked him, “Have you not had voters talk to you specifically about what the president is doing?”

That answer floored me. “Never?”

Article continues below this ad

“Literally never comes up,” Hilton boasted. “It’s ‘What are we going to do about the gas prices?’ Right now in California, you’ll see gas prices in the $5 to $6 range. If you go to Texas today, they’re in the $3 range. Same country, same president, same Iran war going on, vastly different gas prices. That’s entirely due to the policies that Democrats have pursued in California.”

He’s partially correct, given that California’s gas prices are high partially because the state has the highest gas tax in the country, and its fuel standards increase costs for producers. But he again fails to acknowledge the role the Trump administration has played in driving up prices nationwide. It’s a form of denial that he’s shown many times over, from asking voters to ignore Trump’s endorsement of him after he accepted it, to attempting to soften his affection for other members of the MAGA herd, including the late Charlie Kirk. Hilton came to our meeting sporting a wristband honoring the fallen white supremacist. I asked him why he had it.

“He was a good friend of mine, and someone gave it to me,” Hilton said about that. “So I just kept it.”

Article continues below this ad

“Did you like his way of going about things, because he was rather open about his views on race.”

“I’m not sure what you’re referring to.”

“Well, he was a friend of mine. I’m sure we all agree that we are friends with many people. That doesn’t mean we agree with 100% of everything they’ve ever said or done. You can still be friends with someone, just as I am with many Democrats. Don’t agree with them, but we’re friends.”

Article continues below this ad

Do not count Becerra, the Democratic candidate, as one such friend. Hilton made sure to get in his jabs at Becerra in between all of my nagging questions. “We haven’t even talked about all the disqualifying factors for my opponent, who, in the words of [former Biden official] Susan Rice is ‘an idiot.’ You can’t have an idiot as governor of California.” 

I asked if he thought Becerra was especially idiotic given the current level of stupidity in the Trump administration, but he quickly sidestepped. 

“I don’t know. You’d have to ask Susan Rice. I don’t know why she called him an idiot.”

Article continues below this ad

“Well, you just said it was a great quote about him, so you must think he’s an idiot, too.”

“I’m just telling you what people who have experience of working with him say. She also called him a ‘bitch-ass,’ whatever that means exactly.”

“I think you know what a bitch-ass means.”

“I actually, truly don’t know exactly what that means.”

Article continues below this ad

He must have learned in the interim. Because one week ago, Hilton faced off against Becerra in the only televised gubernatorial debate prior to the election. There, he brought up the “bitch-ass” comment from Rice directly to his opponent. He also constantly took umbrage anytime Becerra tried to link him to the president.

“All you ever say is ‘Trump, Trump, Trump,’” he admonished Becerra. “That’s nothing but an insult to every Californian who is desperate for something to change in this state.”

Article continues below this ad

If voters here are desperate for a change, they’re not buying Hilton as the face of it. Two weeks after Labor Day, he is now down against Becerra by 25 points. I don’t think he’s going to win this election. Because when you’re a Republican, there’s no hiding it.
